summary: Codex declares **no provisioning infrastructure at all** — no Terraform, Kubernetes, Helm, compose, CloudFormation or Ansible file exists in the tree. What it does declare, in **8 files**, is how the software is *developed*: two devcontainer profiles over three single-stage Ubuntu 24.04 Dockerfiles, and a Nix flake covering four platforms. All three images run as a non-root user in their final stage, no credential is passed as a build arg, and the 'secure' devcontainer's unusual capability grants are justified line by line in a README that also documents the DNS-exfiltration hole it cannot close. The delivery infrastructure — a Cloudflare R2 bucket named in a script, four GitHub environments, a self-hosted runner fleet, an Azure signing vault — is consumed by name and declared nowhere, but most of it belongs to other parties, so that is a boundary rather than a gap. The one real weakness is pinning of pulled content: **none of the 5 image references is digest-pinned**, two devcontainer features ride `:latest`, and three `curl | sh` installers run at build time — inside a repository where 195 of 195 GitHub Actions are SHA-pinned and pnpm enforces a release-age floor. Everything above `info` is developer-scoped and rated `low`; nothing here builds or publishes an image.

coverage_gaps: GitHub deployment environments: codex-r2-publisher, issue-triage, pypi, dev-website-vercel-deploy
Azure Key Vault used for macOS and Windows code signing
the ChatGPT backend-api the CLI calls

The script's privileged_candidates=9 is accurate but counts individual runArgs lines (7 cap-adds plus 2 security-opts) in one file, not 9 mechanisms - reported as one hardening/privileges finding. findings.title: Eight environment-definition files, no provisioning IaC
findings.description: A direct filesystem glob (not the Sokrates index, which excludes `.github/`) finds **8 infrastructure files** and they are all *environment definitions*, never provisioning code. Three Dockerfiles: `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` (the arm64 contributor image), `.devcontainer/Dockerfile.secure` (the customer-oriented profile) and `.github/workflows/Dockerfile.bazel`. Two devcontainer manifests: `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` and `.devcontainer/devcontainer.secure.json`. Three Nix files: `flake.nix`, `flake.lock` and `codex-rs/default.nix`. There is **no Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, CDK, Kubernetes manifest, Helm chart, Kustomize overlay, Ansible playbook, docker-compose file, serverless config or Vagrantfile anywhere in the tree** — every one of those globs returns zero. This is the correct shape for the artifact: Codex is a CLI distributed as signed binaries and npm packages, so it has environments to *develop in*, not environments to *provision*. `tech-stack-scan` already records that Docker and Nix are in use; this scanner reads what those files declare.

evidence.note: contributor devcontainer builds the local Dockerfile

evidence.snippet: description = "Development Nix flake for OpenAI Codex CLI";
evidence.note: the flake is explicitly a development flake, not a deployment one
the third and last Dockerfile

findings.title: Nothing this repository runs could be rebuilt from it, and it does not need to be
findings.description: Asked the load-bearing question — *if this repository were the only thing left, what could be rebuilt?* — the answer is: **the developer environment, completely; the delivery infrastructure, not at all**. The release pipeline mutates named infrastructure that no file here declares. `publish_r2_release.py` writes into a Cloudflare R2 bucket hard-coded as `releases` under prefix `codex`; nothing creates that bucket, its lifecycle rules, or its public-read policy. Four GitHub deployment environments are referenced by name — `codex-r2-publisher`, `issue-triage`, `pypi` and `dev-website-vercel-deploy` — with their protection rules, reviewers and secrets living in GitHub settings, not in code. The full CI/release matrix requests **self-hosted runner groups by name** (`${{ github.event.repository.name }}-runners`, `…-linux-x64-xl`); no code here provisions those machines. The Azure Key Vault used for macOS and Windows code signing, the npm and PyPI registries, the WinGet repository, the Vercel project behind `developers.openai.com`, and the ChatGPT backend the CLI talks to are all consumed by name and declared nowhere. Nothing here builds or publishes any of the three container images either — `Dockerfile.bazel` in particular is referenced by **no workflow at all** (see `resources/container-images`). Crucially, **this team is not the owner of most of what is missing**: npm, PyPI, WinGet and the ChatGPT backend belong to other parties or other repositories, so their absence is a boundary, not a gap. The genuinely OpenAI-owned pieces that only exist as GitHub and Cloudflare console state are the R2 bucket, the four environments and the self-hosted runner fleet — those would have to be recreated from memory or from a private repository. Per the severity rule this stays `info`: a CLI that consumes hosted infrastructure is not its owner, and `cicd-scan` already owns the question of when these steps run.

evidence.note: the R2 bucket is a hard-coded name; nothing in the repo declares it
self-hosted runner group requested by name, provisioned outside the repo
GitHub environment carrying the R2 write credentials, configured in repo settings

findings.title: Three single-stage images, all Ubuntu 24.04, none of them built by anything here
findings.description: All three Dockerfiles are **single-stage** — the script counts 3 `FROM` lines across 3 files — and all three land on Ubuntu 24.04. `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` is the contributor image: `ubuntu:24.04`, apt build deps plus musl and clang, then `USER ubuntu` before installing Rust into the user's home, `WORKDIR /workspace`, no `ENTRYPOINT`, no `CMD`, no `EXPOSE`, no `HEALTHCHECK` — it is a shell to work in, not a service. `.devcontainer/Dockerfile.secure` starts from `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu-24.04`, adds the firewall toolchain (`iptables`, `ipset`, `dnsutils`, `aggregate`), installs bubblewrap and marks it setuid (`chmod u+s /usr/bin/bwrap`), installs a lockfile-pinned Codex CLI, then drops to `USER vscode`. `.github/workflows/Dockerfile.bazel` is `ubuntu:24.04` plus dotslash, `USER ubuntu`. **Every image runs as a non-root user in its final stage** — `ubuntu`, `vscode`, `ubuntu` respectively — which is the single strongest declared property in this repository's infrastructure. The notable gap is that **nothing in the repository builds or publishes any of them**. A comment in `Dockerfile.bazel` says it was pushed by hand to a personal Docker Hub account, `docker.io/mbolin491/codex-bazel:latest`, with a `TODO` to move somewhere proper — and no workflow references the file or that image, so it is effectively dead weight whose only consumer would be someone running the buildx line in the comment. Separately, two CI jobs run *inside* stock images that no Dockerfile here produces: `rust-release-zsh.yml` sets `image: ubuntu:24.04` and `image: arm64v8/ubuntu:24.04` as job containers, installing build prerequisites as root at job time.

evidence.note: contributor image final-stage user
secure image final-stage user
the CI image is hand-pushed to a personal registry namespace and referenced by no workflow

findings.title: Two devcontainer profiles that differ by an entire security model
findings.description: The two devcontainer manifests are not staging-and-production variants of one environment; they are **two different threat models** sharing a folder, and `.devcontainer/README.md` names the split: `devcontainer.json` is 'for working on this repository', `devcontainer.secure.json` is 'for running Codex inside a project container'. The contributor profile is 31 lines: build the local Dockerfile with context `..`, force `--platform=linux/arm64`, one dotslash feature, two env values (`RUST_BACKTRACE`, `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`), `remoteUser: ubuntu`. No mounts, no capabilities, no lifecycle scripts. The secure profile adds essentially everything else: 4 build args, 9 `runArgs` granting capabilities and unconfining seccomp/AppArmor, `init: true`, 7 named volume and bind mounts, **10 `containerEnv` values plus a `remoteEnv` that forwards the host's `OPENAI_API_KEY` into the container**, and two lifecycle hooks (`postCreateCommand` runs `post_install.py`, `postStartCommand` runs `post_start.sh`, which installs the iptables/ipset egress allowlist). The interesting property is the **egress allowlist as declared configuration**: `OPENAI_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` names 14 hosts (OpenAI API and auth, GitHub and its content CDNs, crates.io, static.rust-lang.org, npm, PyPI) and `init-firewall.sh` default-denies IPv6 outright so the allowlist cannot be bypassed over AAAA. Two things are worth flagging as declaration quality rather than risk. First, `containerEnv` sets **`CODEX_UNSAFE_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX: 1`, a variable that no code in the repository reads** — a grep of the entire tree finds exactly one occurrence, this line. It is either renamed-away or aspirational, and a reader would reasonably believe it disables Codex's sandbox when it does nothing. Second, the README documents a real residual hole in the profile's own words: the firewall does not filter DNS, so 'code from an untrusted repository can exfiltrate data through DNS'. That honesty is unusual and worth preserving. The `remoteEnv` API-key forward is the mechanism only; `configuration-scan` and `security-scan` own the credential itself.
findings.recommendation: Delete `CODEX_UNSAFE_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX` from `devcontainer.secure.json`, or restore the code that reads it. A security-relevant environment variable that no longer has a reader is worse than none, because it advertises a control that is not there.

evidence.note: the only occurrence of this name anywhere in the tree; no code reads it
host API key forwarded into the container by the manifest

evidence.snippet: The firewall does not apply its domain allowlist to DNS traffic, so code from an untrusted repository can exfiltrate data through DNS. This devcontainer does not provide secure DNS resolution. Use it only with trusted repositories. To mitigate DNS exfiltration, implement your own DNS filtering and restrict outbound DNS traffic to the filtered resolver; this does not make untrusted repositories safe because they can still exfiltrate data through allowed HTTPS destinations.
evidence.note: the profile documents its own residual exfiltration channel

findings.title: Nix flake pins its inputs by revision but its Rust toolchain by 'latest'
findings.description: The Nix flake is the third developer-environment mechanism and pins differently from the containers, so it gets its own finding. `flake.nix` declares two inputs — `nixpkgs` from the **`nixos-unstable` rolling channel** and `oxalica/rust-overlay` — across four systems (x86_64/aarch64 for Linux and Darwin). A rolling channel would be unreproducible on its own, but `flake.lock` pins both to exact commits (`nixpkgs` at `bfc1b8a…`, `rust-overlay` at `a1d32c9…`), so a checkout builds the same closure until someone runs `nix flake update`. The residual looseness is *inside* the pinned snapshot: both the package build and the dev shell take `pkgs.rust-bin.stable.latest`, so the Rust version is whatever the locked nixpkgs/rust-overlay pair happens to consider latest — **not the `1.95.0` that `Dockerfile.secure` pins, and not whatever `rust-toolchain.toml` pins for Cargo builds**. Three developer environments in this repository therefore agree on almost everything except the compiler version. `codex-rs/default.nix` is the actual derivation: `cargoLock.lockFile = ./Cargo.lock`, `doCheck = false`, and a `postPatch` that rewrites the placeholder `version = "0.0.0"` — the same version-stamping asymmetry `cicd-scan` found in the release flow, handled here explicitly.
findings.recommendation: Pin the Nix toolchain to the same version the other two environments use — read `rust-toolchain.toml` from the flake (`rust-bin.fromRustupToolchainFile`) instead of `stable.latest`, so all three developer paths compile with one compiler.

evidence.note: rolling channel as input, held steady only by flake.lock
toolchain resolved as 'latest' rather than the pinned 1.95.0
Rust dependencies are lockfile-pinned in the derivation

findings.title: The secure profile trades container isolation for an egress firewall, deliberately and in writing
findings.description: `devcontainer.secure.json` grants **seven Linux capabilities and unconfines both seccomp and AppArmor** in nine `runArgs` lines: `SYS_ADMIN`, `SYS_CHROOT`, `SETUID`, `SETGID`, `SYS_PTRACE`, `NET_ADMIN`, `NET_RAW`, plus `--security-opt=seccomp=unconfined` and `--security-opt=apparmor=unconfined`. Read naively this is the most alarming declaration in the repository — `SYS_ADMIN` with seccomp off is close to container escape. Read in context it is the opposite of careless. `.devcontainer/README.md` explains each grant: the profile 'disables Docker's outer seccomp and AppArmor profiles so bubblewrap can construct Codex's inner sandbox' and 'requires `NET_ADMIN` and `NET_RAW` so the firewall can be installed at startup'. The design is a **deliberate swap of outer isolation for inner isolation**: Docker's generic profile is relaxed so that Codex's own bubblewrap sandbox — the Linux backend `architecture-scan` documents, using `--unshare-user --unshare-net` — can build its namespaces as a non-root user, which is why `Dockerfile.secure` also marks bubblewrap setuid (`chmod u+s /usr/bin/bwrap`). The egress allowlist then constrains what the whole container can reach. Three things keep this at `low` rather than `medium`. The container is developer-facing and never deployed anywhere. The relaxation is confined to the *secure* profile — the default contributor profile has zero `runArgs` beyond `--platform`. And the reasoning is documented next to the declaration rather than discovered by a reader. The genuine residual is that these grants are unconditional: a developer who sets `CODEX_ENABLE_FIREWALL=0` (which `post-start.sh` honours, exiting early with 'Firewall mode: permissive') gets the relaxed container **without** the compensating egress control, and nothing in the manifest prevents that combination. The `vscode` user also has passwordless sudo from the Microsoft base image, which `post_install.py` and `post-start.sh` both rely on — so the non-root `USER vscode` is a smaller boundary than it looks.
findings.recommendation: Make the compensating control non-optional: have `post-start.sh` fail rather than warn when `CODEX_ENABLE_FIREWALL` is not `1`, so the capability grants and the egress allowlist can never be separated. Consider dropping `SYS_PTRACE` unless a debugger genuinely needs it in this profile — it is the one grant the README does not justify.

evidence.note: first of seven capability grants
Docker's default seccomp profile disabled
bubblewrap made setuid so the inner sandbox works for a non-root user

findings.title: Every image reference is a mutable tag; nothing is pinned by digest
findings.description: **Zero of the five image references in the repository are pinned by digest.** Three are base images in Dockerfiles: `ubuntu:24.04` twice and `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu-24.04` once. Two are CI job containers in `rust-release-zsh.yml`: `ubuntu:24.04` and `arm64v8/ubuntu:24.04`. All five are version tags rather than `:latest`, which is the better half of the spectrum — `ubuntu:24.04` moves only as the 24.04 LTS point releases advance — but a tag is still a mutable pointer the publisher can repoint, and none of these is verified by digest or signature at pull time. The contrast with the rest of this repository's supply-chain posture is stark and worth stating plainly: `cicd-scan` found **195 of 195** third-party GitHub Actions pinned to full commit SHAs; pnpm enforces a 7-day `minimumReleaseAge` and `blockExoticSubdeps`; uv sets a 7-day `exclude-newer`; Cargo dependencies are lockfile-pinned and audited by `cargo-deny`. Container images are the one dependency class that escaped that discipline entirely. This stays `low` rather than `medium` under the 'nothing publishes or deploys the artifact' rule: no workflow builds or pushes any of the three images, so the mutable base tags only affect developer machines and the two zsh-build CI jobs. **If the Bazel image were ever wired into CI as its `TODO` intends, this would become `medium`** — a repointed base tag would then silently change what builds release artifacts.
findings.recommendation: Pin the two `ubuntu:24.04` bases and the two zsh job containers by digest (`ubuntu:24.04@sha256:…`) with a renovate-style bot to advance them, matching the SHA-pinning rule already applied to every GitHub Action. The devcontainer base can follow the same pattern.

evidence.note: version tag, not a digest
Microsoft-published base on a mutable tag
CI job container built by no Dockerfile here, also unpinned

findings.title: Three curl-pipe-shell installers and a :latest devcontainer feature inside otherwise locked-down builds
findings.description: Four places pull executable content from the network into an image without verifying it, in a repository that verifies almost everything else. Both devcontainer Dockerfiles install Rust with `curl -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh` — the canonical rustup bootstrap, TLS-protected but with no signature or checksum, and the `.secure` variant at least pins the resulting toolchain to `1.95.0`. `Dockerfile.secure` additionally pipes NodeSource's setup script straight into bash (`curl -fsSL "https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_${NODE_MAJOR}.x" | bash -`), which adds an apt repository and its signing key to the image on the strength of that one TLS connection. Both devcontainer manifests pull `ghcr.io/facebook/devcontainers/features/dotslash:latest` — **an explicitly mutable `:latest` tag on a third-party feature that executes at container build time**, the loosest reference in the repository. `Dockerfile.bazel` is the counter-example that shows the team knows how: it fetches dotslash from a **pinned release URL** (`v0.5.8`), not a rolling tag. The bright spot is the Codex CLI install path in `Dockerfile.secure`, which is genuinely well-provenanced: a dedicated `.devcontainer/codex-install/` boundary with its own lockfile, `corepack pnpm install --prod --frozen-lockfile`, a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` carrying `minimumReleaseAge: 10080` and `blockExoticSubdeps`, and a build-time assertion that the lockfile's `@openai/codex` version equals the `CODEX_NPM_VERSION` build arg. That is the standard the curl-pipes fall short of. Developer-scope keeps this `low`; the `:latest` feature is the piece most worth fixing because it is the only reference here that can change without anyone editing a file.
findings.recommendation: Pin the dotslash devcontainer feature to a released version instead of `:latest` in both manifests — it is a one-word change that removes the only silently-mutable dependency in the developer environments. For the shell installers, download to a file, verify a published checksum, then execute, as `Dockerfile.bazel` already does for dotslash.

evidence.note: third-party build-time feature on a mutable :latest tag
remote script piped to bash, adding an apt repo and key
the same tool fetched from a pinned release URL - the pattern the others should follow

findings.title: No secret reaches a build, but the whole repository is the build context with no .dockerignore
findings.description: The build-secret surface is clean and the build-context surface is not. Six `ARG`s exist across the two devcontainer Dockerfiles and **every one is a non-sensitive build parameter**: `DEBIAN_FRONTEND`, `TZ`, `NODE_MAJOR`, `RUST_TOOLCHAIN`, `CODEX_NPM_VERSION`. No credential is passed as a build arg, no `--mount=type=secret` is needed, and no `COPY` brings a key into an image — `Dockerfile.secure` copies only three named install files and three named scripts, never the tree. The context, however, is wide open. **There is no `.dockerignore` anywhere in the repository**, and both devcontainer manifests set `"context": ".."`, so the Docker daemon receives the entire checkout — roughly **61 MB across 6,400 files** in a clean clone, with `MODULE.bazel.lock` (1.5 MB), `.github/codex-cli-splash.png` (0.8 MB), a TUI test fixture (0.8 MB) and two app-server JSON schemas (1.2 MB together) as the largest items. Because nothing does a `COPY . .`, none of that reaches an image layer — the cost is transfer time on every rebuild, plus the fact that anything a developer happens to leave in their working tree (`.env` files, `personal/`, a `~/.codex` copy) is handed to the daemon. `.gitignore` covers those for git but a build context ignores `.gitignore` entirely. The README's manual `docker build ./.devcontainer` uses the small folder as context instead and is unaffected, which means **the two documented ways to build the same image disagree about the context** — a reader following the README sees none of this. This is `info`: no secret is exposed and no image is published, so it is a fact about the build, not a risk.

evidence.note: build context is the repository root; no .dockerignore exists to filter it
representative build arg - a version, not a credential
the documented manual build uses the .devcontainer folder as context, unlike the manifests

findings.title: Posture: complete developer environments, zero provisioning code, and one dependency class left out of an otherwise excellent supply chain
findings.description: **What could be rebuilt from this repository: the way Codex is developed. What could not: anything it is delivered through.** Three developer-environment mechanisms — a contributor devcontainer, a firewalled 'secure' devcontainer, and a Nix flake — are declared completely enough that a new contributor on Linux, macOS, x86 or arm can reproduce a working toolchain from a clean clone. That is the whole of the infrastructure code: **there is no Terraform, no Kubernetes, no Helm, no compose file, no CloudFormation, no Ansible anywhere in the tree**, and for a CLI shipped as signed binaries that is the right answer rather than a gap. The delivery side is entirely console state: a Cloudflare R2 bucket named `releases` in a Python script, four GitHub deployment environments, a self-hosted runner fleet requested by label, an Azure Key Vault for code signing, and registries owned by other parties. Most of that is not this team's to own, so `coverage` rates it `info` — but the R2 bucket, the environments and the runner group are OpenAI's and exist only as clicks. **Strongest declared property**: every one of the three images runs as a non-root user in its final stage, and the secure profile's relaxations are justified line by line in a README that also admits the residual DNS exfiltration channel it cannot close. Infrastructure that documents its own weaknesses is rarer than infrastructure that has none. **Weakest declared property**: pinning of pulled content. Five image references, none by digest; two devcontainer features on `:latest`; three `curl | sh` installers. This sits inside a repository where 195 of 195 GitHub Actions are SHA-pinned, pnpm enforces a release-age floor, and `cargo-deny` audits every crate — containers are simply the class that the discipline never reached. The three highest-leverage changes, in order: pin `ghcr.io/facebook/devcontainers/features/dotslash:latest` to a version in both manifests (`hardening/build-provenance` — the only reference here that can change with nobody editing a file); pin the Ubuntu bases and the two zsh CI job containers by digest (`hardening/image-pinning`); and delete the dead `CODEX_UNSAFE_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX` variable that advertises a control the code no longer has (`environments/dev-environment`). One piece of housekeeping worth its own line: `.github/workflows/Dockerfile.bazel` is referenced by no workflow and carries a `TODO` about a personal Docker Hub account — either wire it up properly or remove it, because a build file nothing builds will rot silently.

evidence.note: the developer-environment story, which is the whole of this repository's IaC
the primary environment definition
